A CASE REPORT OF ATYPICAL STIFF
PERSON SYNDROME WITH CRANIAL
NERVE INVOLVEMENT PRECEEDING THE
DIAGNOSIS OF A HIGH GRADE
LYMPHOMA
N. Aquilina 1, M. Vella 1, A. Galea Debono 1,
D.J. Camilleri 2
1 Department of Neurology, 2 Department of Haematology,
Mater Dei Hospital, Msida, Malta
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is characterised by progressive
muscle rigidity and spasms primarily affecting the axial
musculature and lower limbs. Paraneoplastic SPS has also
been recognised, mainly associated with breast carcinoma
and anti-ampiphysin antibodies, and manifests clinically by
predominant arm and neck involvement. We report the case
of a 64-year-old gentleman, who presented with a 4-week
history of dysarthria, dysphagia, choking on liquids and
inability to protrude his tongue. Examination revealed a
spastic tongue, masseter spasm and opisthotonus as well as
a spastic gait. Ophthalmoparesis and ptosis followed shortly.
Tactile stimuli precipitated reflex spasms for which he
needed ventilatory support, and a diagnosis of suspected
cephalic tetanus was made. Blood and CSF for antibodies
including onconeuronal antibodies, anti-GAD and anti-
ampiphysin antibodies were all negative. After a prolonged
period of assisted ventilation and several treatment regimes
including magnesium, diazepam, carbamazepine and
baclofen his clinical condition improved somewhat, though
occasional episodes of chest spasms on stimulation and
laryngeal spasms with choking persisted. Six months
following the initial diagnosis of tetanus, a rapidly enlarging
axillary mass was noted and a tissue diagnosis of high grade
T-cell lymphoma was made. On initiation of high dose
chemotherapy, his neurological signs and symptoms
improved significantly. This case highlights the unusual
presentation of antibody-negative paraneoplastic stiff
person syndrome with cranial nerve involvement and
emphasises the need for identification of other antibodies
associated specifically with lymphoma.
